recentItems.title: German chancellor faces pressure after far-right AfD wins state election
recentItems.description:
(7 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTIONS SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Berlin, Germany - 7 September 2026
1. SOUNDBITE (English) David Keyton, The Associated Press: 
++STARTS ON SOUNDBITE++
"A small eastern German state has delivered a political shock with consequences far beyond Germany. The AfD, classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as an extremist group, fell just short of an outright majority in Sunday's regional elections. As unwieldy coalition talks begin, it may still find a path to lead Germany’s first far-right-state government since the Nazi era. That would mark a watershed for Europe’s biggest economy—and potentially destabilize the national coalition government. The international reaction shows the divide: Elon Musk congratulated the AfD, while US President Donald Trump shared the result without comment. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk condemned anyone celebrating it. The big loser of Sunday’s election was the German Chancellor’s own party, the CDU that saw its support cut roughly in half. That’s a scathing result and attention now turns to the Chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and whether Germany’s political firewall against the far right can hold."

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Magdeburg, Germany - 6 September 2026
2. Various of  Alternative for Germany (AfD) supporters cheering and celebrating 
3. AfD regional leader Björn Höcke singing UPSOUND (German): “Such a day, so beautiful as today”
4. Mid of people filming on mobile phones 

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Magdeburg, Germany - 6 September 2026
5. AfD candidate for governor in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, and his wife, Julia Siegmund, arriving on stage 
6. Various of audience 
7. Siegmund and officials singing German national anthem

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Magdeburg, Germany -  7 September 2026
8. Newspapers on display in Magdeburg, Germany, highlighting morning reactions
9. German Bild newspaper headline reads (German): "Joy and Pain"
10. German Magdeburger Volksstimmer headline reads (German): "triumph for AfD, CDU in free fall"
11. German Sueddeutsche Zeitung headline reads( German): "AfD wins in Saxony-Anhalt"
12. Various of state parliament in Magdeburg, European and German flags displayed 
STORYLINE:
A small eastern German state has delivered a political shock with consequences far beyond Germany. 

The AfD, classified by Germany's domestic intelligence agency as an extremist group, fell just short of an outright majority in Sunday's regional elections. 

As unwieldy coalition talks begin, it may still find a path to lead Germany’s first far-right-state government since the Nazi era. That would mark a watershed for Europe’s biggest economy—and potentially destabilize the national coalition government. 

The international reaction shows the divide: Elon Musk congratulated the AfD, while Donald Trump shared the result without comment. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk condemned anyone celebrating it.

The big loser of Sunday’s election was the German Chancellor’s own party, the CDU that saw its support cut roughly in half.

That’s a scathing result and attention now turns to the Chancellor Friedrich Merz—and whether Germany’s political firewall against the far right can hold.

recentItems.title: Several killed in Israeli airstrikes on village in southern Lebanon
recentItems.description:
(7 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS   
Kfar Rumman, Lebanon -  07 September 2026
1. Various of bulldozer clearing out rubble at site of Israeli strike
2. Various of civil defense and Lebanese army at site of strike and searching rubble
3. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Wafaa Ahmad, neighbor of targeted building:
“I was sleeping in this room, and my sons were sleeping upstairs. At 1:30 in the morning we heard loud booms, we hadn’t heard a missile or any aircraft, just booms. I was in bed and the rubble and glass were falling on me and my daughter. I started wondering when I would die. The roof where my sons were started falling on me. The smoke filled the house, we were suffocating. I crawled out and when I reached here, I started yelling for my sons, I was calling out to Wissam, Ali and Hassan, until I heard them tell me they’re ok.”
4. Pan of destruction inside property
5. Man walking through destroyed property
6. Various of Lebanese army at site
7. Various of bulldozer clearing out rubble, Lebanese army, civil defense and residents gathered
8. Lebanese army patrolling, vehicles
9. Ambulance
STORYLINE:
Israel’s air force carried out two airstrikes on a southern Lebanese village early Monday, killing at least nine people and wounding others, including women and children, Lebanon’s Health Ministry said.

The Ministry said one of the strikes hit a building in Kfar Rumman, killing eight people, including a child and two women. 

It added that 11 people were also wounded, including four children and two women.

The ministry said that another strike on a car in the village killed a paramedic with the Lebanese Islamic Risala Scout Association and wounded two others.

Monday’s strikes came amid a new round of escalation between Israel and the militant Hezbollah group despite a truce reached more than two months ago. 

A U.S.-brokered truce between Israel and Hezbollah as been repeatedly violated with Israel carrying out airstrikes in Lebanon and Hezbollah firing drones at Israeli troops.

Lebanon and Israel in June signed a U.S.-mediated framework deal under which Israeli forces were to withdraw from southern Lebanon in exchange for the disarmament of Hezbollah.

However, little progress has been made in its implementation.

Hezbollah is not a party to the Lebanon-Israel talks and has said it will not give up its weapons in any area north of southern Lebanon’s Litani River. 

Israeli officials, meanwhile, have said they will not withdraw unless Hezbollah is disarmed throughout the country.

recentItems.title: Nepal holds day of mourning to remember flood victims
recentItems.description:
(7 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTIONS SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Dhunge, Nuwakot District, Nepal - 7 September 2026
1. Various of a Hindu priest praying for flood victims 
2. Wide of rescuers shouting standing outside damaged buildings; UPSOUND (Nepali)  "Hear me, hear me, hear me. We are search and rescue people. If you are hearing us please call for help”
3. Various of rescue workers next to flood damaged buildings
4. Wide of damaged buildings 

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Kathmandu, Nepal - 7 September 2026
5. Various of family members performing symbolic funeral 
6. Relatives of people who were working hydropower plants and missing during the flooding gather in Kathmandu demanding the government speed up rescue efforts
7. SOUNDBITE (Nepali) Sumana Shrestha, wife of missing geologist:
“We are here because we have heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already.”
8. SOUNDBITE (Nepali) Mahesh Prasad Shrestha, brother of missing engineer:
“Our people were buried in the project office, and it was only on the sixth or seventh day the authorities sent a small JCV (excavator) by a small helicopter. They should have ordered big helicopters from places (such as) China or India to fly equipment.”
9. Nepal’s national flag at half-staff to mark a day of national mourning of the people killed in the floods
STORYLINE:
Nepal held a day of mourning Monday to remember people who died in the August 26 floods with government offices lowering flags and family members concluding mourning rituals.

Search efforts were continuing for hundreds of people who are still missing.

Monday is the 13th day since the flooding that has killed over 1,300 people in Nepal and Tibet and left some 5,000 missing including foreigners, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

In Hindu-dominated Nepal, mourning periods last 13 days, in which close family members stay home and relatives visit to pay respects. 

On the final or 13th day, rituals are held to pray for the departed souls.

Several people whose family members are still missing have performed symbolic funerals with mourning rituals. In Hindu tradition, cremation is an important final rite, and for some families, performing the ceremony even without the bodies of their loved ones provides a sense of spiritual release.

In Kathmandu, family members wanted information near the prime minister's offices. 

They called on key ministries to demand a faster search and rescue for the hundreds of people who were working on hydropower plants and were either swept by the rushing river or buried by the debris.

AP video shot by Upendra Mansingh, Niranjan Shrestha and Yar Dasin

recentItems.title: Germans react as AfD party wins regional election short of majority
recentItems.description:
(7 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Magdeburg, Germany -  7 September 2026
1. Pedestrians and cyclists on street
2. Damaged CDU election poster 
3. Newspapers on display in Magdeburg, Germany, highlighting morning reactions
4. German Bild newspaper headline reads (German): "Joy and Pain"
5. German Magdeburger Volksstimmer headline reads (German): "triumph for AfD, CDU in free fall"
6. German Sueddeutsche Zeitung headline reads( German): "AfD wins in Saxony-Anhalt"
7. Various of state parliament in Magdeburg, European and German flags displayed 
8. SOUNDBITE (German) Horst Walter Boerner, 86-years-old, Magdeburg resident:
"It's terrible for us. I experienced my first World War. I am 86 years old and she (his wife) is 84. And now this is normal, but it has nothing to do with the World War. Nevertheless, everything seems to be coming together strangely here in Europe and especially in Germany. And this whole election, I think, is a fear-driven election, but a certain potential or a certain human kind has influenced this election. And that was foreseeable. You could see it when the AfD gathered. Large crowds were there. That should never have happened."
9. Cyclists passing election posters
10. SOUNDBITE (German) Julia Lukas, Magdeburg resident:
"The party that has now obviously won is not my favorite, if I may say so. Yes, of course. No party can ever get it completely right, but people who have come here because they no longer feel at home elsewhere and have found work and are also working might then be sent away?"
11. Street cleaner operating in front of state parliament
12. SOUNDBITE (German) Christa Wielich, born Dessau, visits Magdeburg:
"The federal government really needs to think hard about whether much has to change. I don't know. But now I'm going to look at Saxony-Anhalt. I was born in Dessau. That's why I'm here now. Uh, yes, we have to digest this."
13. Various of heart-shaped sculpture in Magdeburg's square as people walk by, capturing morning reactions
STORYLINE:
The far-right Alternative for Germany party has surged to a resounding victory in a regional election. 

But it fell a little short of winning a majority Sunday in its quest to form the country’s first far-right state government since World War II. 

The party of Germany’s unpopular leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, slumped to a disastrous result in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. 

The anti-migration and Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany’s candidate for governor said "we have written history” and the party had a clear mandate to govern.

People in Magdeburg were shocked by yesterday's election results.

Horst Walter Boerner who is 86 years old and had experienced world war felt terrible.

Boerner said, "Nevertheless, everything seems to be coming together strangely here in Europe and especially in Germany. And this whole election, I think, is a fear-driven election, but a certain potential or a certain human kind has influenced this election. And that was foreseeable."

He added, " That should never have happened."

Even though Saxony-Anhalt is one of Germany's smaller states and only 2.1 million people live there, the election received outsized attention, not just in the country but also internationally. 

Unlike other countries in Europe, modern Germany hasn’t yet had a far-right or right-wing populist party leading a national, state or major-city government — and due to the country's Nazi past, far-right movements have always received strong scrutiny here.

However, not everyone was worried about the victorious emergence of AfD.

recentItems.title: Alejandro Fernández draws fans to Mexico City's Arre music festival
recentItems.description:
(7 Sep 2026) 
ASSOCIATED PRESS
Mexico City - 6 September 2026
++ NIGHT SHOTS ++
1. Alejandro Fernández performing at Arre Pepsi Black festival
2. Wide of stage
3. Pull from fan recording on phone to Fernández performing
4. Fernández performing
5. Fan singing along to song
6. Various of fans singing and dancing
7. Fernández performing
8. Fan raising cowboy hat 
9. Various of fans watching show
10. Band performing
11. Fans recording on phones
12. Fernández shown on giant screen
13. SOUNDBITE (Spanish) Ulises Chino, computer engineer:
"The rain was really heavy. We took shelter under a tent, but as soon as it eased up, we came back out to keep enjoying the music."
14. Various of workers pumping water out of flooded road at festival venue
15. Pan on people arriving 
16. Various of people arriving
17. SOUNDBITE (Spanish) Andrés Demich, chef, and Vanessa Oyarzún, actress:
Demich: "We really like the genre (regional Mexican music)."
Oyarzún: "We do."
Demich: "We really like the genre, so whenever we go to a palenque show or a banda music festival, we always try to dress something like this."
18. Various of artist performing 
19. Various of people arriving
20. Man saying hi to camera as others walk away
STORYLINE:
Mexican singer Alejandro Fernández performed Sunday night at the Arre Pepsi Black festival in Mexico City, as fans sang and danced through a rain-soaked evening.

Fernández took the stage at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on the second day of the festival, which brought together performers from across regional Mexican music and other popular genres.

Heavy rain flooded parts of the festival venue, where workers pumped water from a roadway as the event continued.

Earlier in the day, the severe weather forced organizers to temporarily suspend the festival for nearly an hour. 

Messages projected on the stage screens informed the crowd that the concert was paused due to adverse weather conditions, prompting many to seek refuge in food areas before the music could resume.

"The rain was really heavy. We took shelter under a tent, but as soon as it eased up, we came back out to keep enjoying the music," said festival goer and computer engineer Ulises Chino.

Festival-goers continued arriving despite the wet conditions, with some embracing clothing associated with the music they came to hear.

Chef Andrés Demich and actress Vanessa Oyarzún said their outfits, which featured classic cowboy hats and western-style leather jackets, reflected their enthusiasm for regional Mexican music.

"We really like the genre, so whenever we go to a palenque show or a banda music festival, we always try to dress something like this," Demich said, referring to the traditional circular arenas that frequently host intimate, center-ring concerts for regional artists.

The two-day festival began Saturday and featured dozens of performers, with Fernández, Los Tucanes de Tijuana, Eslabon Armado and La Sonora Dinamita among those listed for Sunday's program.

AP Video by Martín Silva Rey

recentItems.title: Jamaica takes case for slavery reparations from UK to King Charles III
recentItems.description:
(7 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
London - 6 September 2026
1. Various of Culture Minister of Jamaica Olivia Grange singing and dancing during the church service 
2. Pan of church service
3. Close of church service pamphlet
4. Mid of Grange speaking during the service
5. SOUNDBITE (English) Olivia Grange, Culture Minister of Jamaica:
"I'm here as head of a delegation from Jamaica representing the people of Jamaica to file a petition inviting the King to refer three questions that we're asking to the Privy Council to make a determination how we address reparatory justice for the enslavement of our ancestors. And we are hoping that those questions will be answered so we can determine next steps going forward. The petition speaks to if it was lawful, if the chattel enslavement was also lawful and if there should be a remedy for what was done to our enslaved ancestors."
6. Various of Grange placing a flower pot as an offering inside church 
7. Wide of people attending the service
8. Various of Grange interacting with other delegations 
9. SOUNDBITE (English) Olivia Grange, Culture Minister of Jamaica:
"Yes, it is historic for Jamaica. We have been working on a reparatory justice initiative for a long time. And we have finally reached a point where that we have been able to file the petition. And for us, it's a strong statement on behalf of persons who want to see justice done. And Jamaicans are very positive about this initiative. We are operating on a mandate from Parliament, where a motion was moved in Parliament and unanimously supported by both sides of the political divide. That we should seek reparations, that we should create a roadmap to determining reparatory justice. And we have reached that point, and we are very happy that today, we are part of history by being able to say we've reached a point where we can file a petition and we await the results."
10. Top shot of people at the service
11. Close of a woman looking at service pamphlet 
12. SOUNDBITE (English) Olivia Grange, Culture Minister of Jamaica:
"Although we were colonized by the UK, once we got our independence, we established diplomatic relations with the UK. So, we have a respectful relationship between both countries, a long-standing relationship, and we expect that to continue. In relation to the wrongs that were done, we want answers and we do not expect that this initiative will affect bilateral relations which now exist in the UK. What we have done, we have taken a legal path, it's not a political path it's a legal path. We have three questions to ask and we are asking those questions and expecting answers. Once we get those answers, then our attorneys or lawyers will determine what the next move is."
13. Mid of Grange interacting with other delegations
14. Various of people singing and dancing
15. Various of service pamphlets 
STORYLINE:
Jamaica is taking its campaign for Britain to pay reparations for the ravages of the trans-Atlantic slave trade to King Charles III.

Using legal traditions that stretch back to the early days of the British Empire, Jamaica will on Monday petition the king to refer a series of questions about slavery and the U.K.’s responsibility to pay damages to a committee of the Privy Council, which serves as the highest court for former colonies that retain ties to the British legal system.

While the petition is formally addressed to the king, Charles has no personal say on whether it will be referred to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and he will act on the advice of the government.

recentItems.title: Grossi and IAEA governors meet in Vienna for regular talks on nuclear issues
recentItems.description:
(7 Sep 2026) 
RESTICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Vienna, Austria – 7 September 2026
1. International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) director general Rafael Grossi arriving for board meeting
2. Close of Grossi
3. Wide of Grossi surrounded by photographers
4. Mid of Grossi 
5. Wide of boardroom
6. Mid of delegates
7. Mid of United States ambassador Preston Wells Griffith
8. Close of Griffith
9. Wide of boardroom
10. Griffith and delegates looking at laptop
11. Wide of boardroom
STORYLINE:
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is holding its scheduled board of governors meeting on Monday. 

Last week the United States, Britain, France and Germany drafted a resolution for possible consideration by the board of governors of the U.N. nuclear watchdog that seeks to refer Iran to the U.N. Security Council for failure to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations, diplomats say.

Under those obligations, which are part of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, Iran is legally bound to declare all nuclear material and activities and allow inspectors of the Vienna-based IAEA to verify that none of it is being diverted from peaceful uses.

The diplomatic move has been under consideration since June 2025 when the IAEA board found Iran officially in noncompliance with its nonproliferation obligations for the first time in 20 years — one day before the U.S. and Israel launched attacks against Iran’s nuclear sites.

The possible referral of Iran to the U.N. Security Council shifts the responsibility to a higher authority that is able to enact further legally binding measures, including sanctions or asset freezes.

Diplomats say that the resolution is still under negotiation and has not yet been formally submitted to the board. 

The text of the draft resolution may therefore still change, as board members still have the opportunity to suggest amendments.

Once formally submitted, it will be put to a vote during the meeting.

AP video by Philipp Jenne

recentItems.title: España: Los abanicos tradicionales cobran protagonismo durante las olas de calor
recentItems.description:
(7 Sep 2026) 
SLUG: Evergreen España Abanicos Calor SP¨
Source: ASSOCIATED PRESS
No additional restrictions beyond those terms outlined in your license agreement.
Vídeo de AP grabado por Manu Fernández y Laura León.

España: Los abanicos tradicionales cobran protagonismo durante las olas de calor

============================================
ASSOCIATED PRESS
Madrid, España — 29 de agosto de 2026
1. Diversas imágenes de personas llevando abanicos por la calle.
2 SOUNDBITE (Español) Macarena Giménez, usuaria de abanico:
++Parte Superpuesta con Tomas 1,3++
“He venido a Madrid, estoy viviendo en Londres. La verdad es que utilizo el abanico porque es que hace una calor aquí en Madrid con 35 grados que yo esto no lo soporto. Ya no soy española parece”.
3. Mujer sentada usando abanico.
4. David González usando abanico. 
5 Mujeres caminando con abanico

6. SOUNDBITE (Español) David González, usuario de abanico:
++Partes Superpuestas con Tomas 4,5,7++
 “Me gusta usar el abanico porque a lo largo del día con el calor que hace me proporciona mucho bienestar y aire fresco. Al principio me daba un poco de vergüenza porque es un articulo que se relaciona sobre todo con la mujer, pero reconozco que tiene su funcionalidad y al fin te dejas un poco de prejuicios y yo voy con el a todas partes”.

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Madrid, España — 25 de agosto de 2026

7. Abanicos en el escaparate de una tienda
8. Mujer mirando abanicos en una tienda
9.  SOUNDBITE (Español) Javier Llerandi, propietario de la tienda Casa de Diego:
++Partes Superpuestas con Tomas 7,8, 10,11++ 
“Nuestro principal cliente es el madrileño, luego el turista nacional y luego el turista extranjero. Nosotros vivimos del calor; antiguamente solo se vendían abanicos en verano. Con la afluencia de turismo en Madrid cada vez mayor pues vendemos abanicos todo el año e indudablemente las olas de calor a este negocio le vienen bien”.

10. Vendedora de abanico en una tienda
11. Surtido de abanicos


STORYLINE:
A medida que las sucesivas olas de calor en Europa occidental elevaban las temperaturas a niveles extremos este verano, el abanico, el tradicional accesorio plegable de mano, se ha convertido en un elemento esencial, adoptado tanto por jóvenes como por mayores, en España o en otros lugares. 

David González, también se abanicaba por las calles de Madrid. "Al principio me sentía un poco cohibido, porque es algo que se asocia principalmente con las mujeres, pero debo admitir que cumple su función y además alegra mi día", dijo González, de 53 años. 

El abanico llegó a Europa a través del comercio portugués con Asia en el siglo XV. 

A mediados del siglo XVII, el pintor español Diego Velázquez creó su enigmática obra "La dama del abanico", en la que una mujer vestida de negro posa con lo que parece ser un delicado abanico de madera. 

En el siglo XIX, su uso estaba muy extendido entre la aristocracia española. 

A medida que los abanicos se ponían de moda en las cortes europeas, España desarrolló su propio gusto e industria en torno a ellos. 

Hoy en día, tiendas especializadas como Casa de Diego en Madrid, así como los quioscos  registran fuertes ventas ante el calor sofocante. 

Con un simple movimiento de muñeca, genera una brisa sorprendentemente intensa. 

Desde España, el abanico viajó a América Latina. En el siglo XIX, las bailaoras de flamenco comenzaron a incorporarlo a sus actuaciones, influenciadas por los estilos musicales y de baile cubanos. 



ANNE MARIE GARCIA, ASSOCIATED PRESS

recentItems.title: 'The Pitt' star Ernest Harden Jr. wins first Emmy after 50 years of acting
recentItems.description:
(7 Sep 2026) 
ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Los Angeles -  6 September 2026
1. Mid of Shailene Woodley posing with her Emmy
2. Wide of Shailene Woodley walking with her Emmy
3. SOUNDBITE (English) Shailene Woodley /Actor:
"I felt like we all did something special together just by means of the way that the filmmakers, John, Glenn, and Ken, they gave so much trust to me as a newcomer, as somebody who didn't know the family already. And I immediately felt very comfortable. I think because of the environment that we felt on set, it really translated onto the screen. And it's been a highlight of my career in every way."
4. Mid of Shailene Woodley holding an Emmy award 
5. Mid of Shailene Woodley posing with her mother 
6. SOUNDBITE (English) Shailene Woodley - Actor:
"What's going through my head is I'm like, 'What did I say on stage?' I was so blacked out like, what? I called everybody clowns. No, I mean, yeah, I guess it is like I started acting when was five years old. And so it's been a lifelong journey, a 30-year journey. And like I just said, it is a team effort. As an artist, a painter, you can really claim 100% of that work is your own. But this is what I'm able to do and what I do every day is a byproduct of the friends that I have in my life and the auditions that my mom took me to and the acting teachers and coaches that I've had through the years and my incredible team, my managers and my agents. Everyone who holds me to a standard that reminds me of who I am and who I want to be in the world, that helps me stay true to the artistic endeavors that I want to pour my life into."

recentItems.title: Mourners pay respects to war criminal Mladic in Serbia
recentItems.description:
(7 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Belgrade, Serbia - 7 August 2026
1. Coffin and framed picture of Ratko Mladic 
2. Various of people bowing in front of coffin
3. Candles  
4. SOUNDBITE (Serbian) Milan Dobric, mourner: 
“He was a man who gave everything in his life for Serbian people In Kosovo, in Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia. I am glad that this morning people are coming to pay special respect.” 
5. Various of people lighting candles
6. SOUNDBITE (Serbian) Radenko Matic, resident:
"He was my commander, and a great man and a soldier.” 
7. Various of queues
8. SOUNDBITE (Serbian) Draginja Pejic, mourner:
"If it weren't for Ratko Mladic, there would be no Republika Srpska. My husband served in the army under Ratko Mladic.” 
9. Mid of coffin in church 
STORYLINE:
Thousands of mourners paid their respects on Monday as the body of Ratko Mladic, the Bosnian Serb commander who died while serving a life sentence for war crimes, was lying in state.

That happened as Serbia defied European Union warnings not to pay official homage to the man found guilty of the continent’s first case of genocide since World War II.  

Mourners had arrived early at the small Serbian Orthodox church of St. Luke in Belgrade to honor the man still viewed as a hero to many Serbs. 

His military's officer's cap and sabre rested on the coffin, which was flanked by Serbian soldiers in fatigues.

Many Serbs consider Mladic a hero despite his conviction for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity by the U.N. tribunal.

“He was a man who gave everything in his life for Serbian people In Kosovo, in Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia," said Milan Dobric, a mourner who traveled to Belgrade from Kosovo. "I am glad that this morning people are coming to pay special respect.” 

AP video by Almir Alic and Marko Drobnjakovic

recentItems.title: Singapore firm Flowtica unveils new AI companion tech at Berlin's IFA
recentItems.description:
(7 Sep 2026) 
ASSOCIATED PRESS
Berlin, Germany - 4 September 2026

1. Various of Mark Yu, chief marketing officer, Flowtica AI, demonstrating Flowtica “Scribe” AI transcription pen, writing note on paper
2. Various of Yu taking photo of handwritten note with smartphone 
3. Close-up of Yu pointing to note on smartphone app
4. SOUNDBITE (English) Mark Yu, chief marketing officer, Flowtica AI:
“We believe that the AI technology should bring more concentration to people and focusing on what they're aiming to finish and get the job done, not getting more distraction and let people lose focus on what they're trying to finish.”

5. Close of Yu pushing record on Flowtica Scribe AI transcription pen
6. Various of Yu scrolling through transcribed recorded conversations on smartphone app
7. SOUNDBITE (English) Mark Yu, chief marketing officer, Flowtica AI:
“For all those people who live by having conversations, like the lawyer, the doctors, and the executives at the company, a long meeting usually brings a long after-meeting hustle. So, with this tool, you don't have to do anything, but just collect it.”

8. Various of new “Verso” AI transcription tool
9. Sign, reading (English): “You Everyday E-paper Sidekick”
10. SOUNDBITE (English) Mark Yu, chief marketing officer, Flowtica AI:
“The AI recorder nowadays, especially those card recorders, they are designed to send you the deliveries after the meeting ends and you have to dig in the app. But with this e-ink display, you can have everything right behind your phone. And when the conversation started, you could have the conversation live on the e-ink display. And when the conversation ends, you can ask for more for your meetings, not just summaries and the transcriptions, but like writing an email for me based on my last conversation, or write me a report with the last meetings in the last month. And everything can be readable on the display.”

11. Sign, reading (English): “You Everyday E-paper Sidekick”
STORYLINE:
LEADIN:

Singapore company Flowtica has unveiled its latest AI productivity devices at Germany’s IFA consumer electronics show in Berlin.

STORYLINE:

It might look like an ordinary pen, but Flowtica’s “Scribe” pen uses the latest AI tech to help workers keep track of their notes and meetings.

After handwriting a note, users can take a picture and it will be automatically transcribed to the company's mobile app. 

It’s also fitted with.a microphone to record meetings and - with the help of AI - generate transcripts, meeting summaries, follow-up suggestions and calendar items.

“We believe that the AI technology should bring more concentration to people and focusing on what they're aiming to finish and get the job done, not getting more distraction and let people lose focus on what they're trying to finish,” says Flowtica’s chief marketing officer Mark Yu.

Yu says their devices are made for “people who live by having conversations”.

“Like the lawyer, the doctors, and the executives at the company,” he says. “A long meeting usually brings a long after meeting hustle. So, with this tool, you don't have to do anything, but just collect it.”

Flowtica is also putting its AI companion tech into these e-ink display devices that can be attached to the back of smartphones.

Unveiled at IFA consumer electronics show, the new “Verso” e-ink device uses magnets to stick to everything from smartphones to fridges and laptops.

It transcribes and summarises meetings directly on its e-ink display, meaning users don’t have to unlock a device or search for a specific file.
